name: Charlemagne
role: King of the Franks (768-814) and Emperor (800-814)
summary: Charlemagne unified most of Western Europe by conquest and used royal capitularies to order the church, the law and the royal estates. His record combines forced conversion and executions for pagan practice in Saxony with a programme of church reform and learning.

sources.title: Capitulary for Saxony (Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae), 750-800
sources.author: Charlemagne (translation as reproduced by Hanover College)

notes:
Most of the 490 statements are null: the sources reached were capitularies and chronicles covering church, law, estates and war, and most statements concern modern issues they never addressed. The Admonitio generalis and the letter De litteris colendis were not read in their Latin or translated text; the Admonitio entry relies on a Wikipedia summary and the letter on a single quoted sentence. Einhard's Verden figure (4,500 beheaded in 782) is reported by Wikipedia from the annals, and the Grant translation of Einhard's chapter 7 was not found to contain it. Inferences are marked low and begin 'Inferred:'.

Merged with an independent gpt-6.1-sol audit: 17 answers taken from it, 19 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

gpt-6.1-sol notes: Independent pass; old audit read only for notes and sources. Full Einhard and Ogg sourcebook downloaded and searched, including the complete De litteris colendis letter rather than only an encyclopedia summary. New economic research used Frankfurt chapter 4 and Nijmegen chapters 9–18 in Latin, checked against Devroey’s scholarly account (full lecture text saved from https://dipot.ulb.ac.be/dspace/bitstream/2013/327081/3/Leedstext.pdf). The capitularies contain his own imperial commands and personal enforcement procedures; they are not treated merely as a ceremonial monarch’s assent to a ministerial program. Einhard is a favorable contemporary biographer and is capped at medium. His favorable generalities about justice do not erase religious coercion, hereditary privilege, compulsory labor and deportation. De Villis governs royal domains rather than prescribing public ownership or planning of the whole economy. No inference from feudal or Christian labels to modern questions. All 490 texts, ten priority propositions and remaining nulls reviewed; economic priorities remain null because the discovered food and credit regulations do not address those wider doctrines. Final specificity review removed international merchant protection as evidence of universal free-trade benefits, foreign treaties as evidence about treaties with nations inside a state, conquest assimilation as evidence about immigrants, and mixed benefice/allod examples as insufficient to settle a universal land-use tenure principle. Every priority remains null.
